t:
a. 
Every economic poison which is distributed, sold, or offered for sale in any Territory or the District of Columbia, or which is shipped or delivered for shipment from any State, Territory, or the District of Columbia to any other State, Territory, or the District of Columbia, or which is received from any foreign country shall be registered with the Secretary: Provided, That products which have the same formula, are manufactured by the same person, the labeling of which contains the same claims, and the labels of which bear a designation identifying the product as the same economic poison may be registered as a single economic poison; and additional names and labels shall be added by supplement statements; the registrant shall file with the Secretary a statement including—

        (1) 
the name and address of the registrant and the name and address of the person whose name will appear on the label, if other than the registrant;
 
        (2) 
the name of the economic poison;
 
        (3) 
a complete copy of the labeling accompanying the economic poison and a statement of all claims to be made for it, including the directions for use; and
 
        (4) 
if requested by the Secretary, a full description of the tests made and the results thereof upon which the claims are based.
  
    b. 
The Secretary, whenever he deems it necessary for the effective administration of this Act, may require the submission of the complete formula of the economic poison. If it appears to the Secretary that the composition of the article is such as to warrant the proposed claims for it and if the article and its labeling and other material required to be submitted comply with the requirements of section 3 of this Act, he shall register it.
 
    c. If it does not appear to the Secretary that the article is such as to warrant the proposed claims for it or if the article and its labeling and other material required to be submitted do not comply with the provisions of this Act, he shall notify the registrant of the manner in which the article, labeling, or other material required to be submitted fail to comply with the Act so as to afford the registrant an opportunity to make the corrections necessary. If, upon receipt of such notice, the registrant insists that such corrections are not necessary and requests in writing that it be registered, the Secretary shall register the article, under protest, and such registration shall be accompanied by a warning, in writing, to the registrant of the apparent failure of the article to comply with the provisions of this Act. In order to protect the public, the Secretary, on his own motion, may at any time, cancel the registration of an economic poison and in lieu thereof issue a registration under protest in accordance with the foregoing procedure. In no event shall registration of an article, whether or not protested, be construed as a defense for the commission of any offense prohibited under section 3 of this Act.
 
    d. Notwithstanding any other provision of this Act, registration is not required in the case of an economic poison shipped from one plant to another plant operated by the same person and used solely at such plant as a constituent part to make an economic poison which is registered under this Act.
 
    e. The Secretary is authorized to cancel the registration of any economic poison at the end of a period of five years following the registration of such economic poison or at the end of any five-year period thereafter, unless the registrant, prior to the expiration of each such five-year period, requests in accordance with regulations issued by the Secretary that such registration be continued in effect.

fable.w: Subsection e contemplates the Secretary issuing regulations to govern requests to continue a registration, and rulemaking authority counts as participation under the definition. The more prominent features of the section (filing for registration, the notice-and-correction exchange, and registration under protest) are an application and appeal-like process for a license, which do not count on their own. The label is a close call because the reference to regulations is incidental rather than an express grant of rulemaking authority.
fable.s: requests in accordance with regulations issued by the Secretary that such registration be continued in effect

qwen_block.w: This section outlines the administrative process for registering economic poisons, which is an application for a license or permit. The definition explicitly states that applications for benefits, grants, contracts, or licenses are not participation. While the registrant has an opportunity to respond to a notice of non-compliance, this is part of the adjudicative process for the application itself, not a consultation or coordination with outside parties regarding a broader federal policy decision.
qwen_block.s: Every economic poison which is distributed, sold, or offered for sale... shall be registered with the Secretary

opus.w: Subsection (e) assumes the Secretary will issue regulations governing renewal requests. The definition counts rulemaking as participation, and Example 6 counted even optional authority to regulate. The tempting 'No' reading treats the section as just a licence-style registration with a protest right by the affected registrant (like Example 11), and those parts alone would not qualify. The regulation reference is what tips it, and it is only implied rather than an explicit grant of rulemaking power.
opus.s: unless the registrant, prior to the expiration of each such five-year period, requests in accordance with regulations issued by the Secretary that such registration be continued in effect
opus.b:
I labelled this **Yes**, but it's a close call (confidence 0.55).

**The tempting reading is "No."** Most of the section is about registering a product, which is a licence-style application. The registrant's right to insist and get registered "under protest" also looks like participation, but it is really a challenge to a decision about the registrant's own product, like the manufacturer's response in Example 11. Neither counts as participation on its own.

**Why I still chose Yes.** Subsection (e) says renewals are requested "in accordance with regulations issued by the Secretary." That assumes the Secretary will write regulations to govern renewal, and the definition counts requiring rulemaking as participation. Example 6 counted even optional authority to regulate.

**Why the call is uncertain.** Example 6 involved an explicit grant of power to issue regulations. Here the regulations are only implied by a passing reference, so labelling this "No" would also be defensible.

qwen_chat.w: This section outlines the requirements for registering an economic poison, which is an application process. The definition explicitly excludes 'applications for benefits, grants, contracts, or licenses' from the scope of participation. The interaction described is the submission of required data for registration and the ability to correct deficiencies in that application, which falls under the application/license trap, not participation in a federal decision-making process like a public hearing or advisory committee.
qwen_chat.s: Every economic poison which is distributed, sold, or offered for sale... shall be registered with the Secretary... the registrant shall file with the Secretary a statement including... (1) the name and address... (2) the name of the economic poison... (3) a complete copy of the labeling... (4) if requested by the Secretary, a full description of the tests...
qwen_chat.b: Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that the requirement for the registrant to submit information and the opportunity to respond to a notice of non-compliance constitutes "participation" because it involves interaction between an outside party (the manufacturer) and the government. However, the definition explicitly states: "It does not include applications for benefits or grants." Registration of a product is analogous to applying for a license or permit. The interaction is part of the application/registration process, not a consultation on a broader policy decision or a public comment period. The "opportunity to make corrections" is part of the administrative review of the application, not a participatory decision-making process involving the public or outside entities in the sense defined (e.g., advisory boards, public hearings, consultation before a decision).
